w10_P4_001678: At a forklift test yard, two steel chains measure 36 links and 126 links. A technician wants the greatest number of links, per section, that divides evenly into both chains with nothing left over, and that number becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a test load with a mass of 64,000 grams. Find the push this load requires, in newtons, then multiply that number by 3, then by 5. Convert what results into kilonewtons, and then subtract 15 from that figure. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001682: The number a crane inspector ultimately reports, in kilonewtons, is 26 less than an earlier kilonewton figure obtained by multiplying a converted force reading by 11. That force, first measured in newtons, is what a 100,000 gram test block exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 105 centimeter cable and a 205 centimeter cable with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001684: A calibration sheet at a satellite-thruster test bay lists two candidate speed readings, in meters per second, for a small test mass: the two numbers add up to 3 and multiply together to give 2. The correct reading is confirmed to be the larger of the two. That speed applies to a test mass weighing 59,000 grams. Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 11. Convert what results into kilojoules, subtract 24 from the figure, and then subtract 11 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001688: The final number a satellite-thruster engineer logs, in kilojoules, is 19 less than an earlier figure, itself obtained by multiplying a kilojoule reading by 7 after subtracting 5 from it. That kilojoule reading came from converting an energy value, in joules, carried by a 59 kilogram test mass moving at a speed numerically equal to a component's acceleration at a certain instant. That acceleration, in meters per second squared, is how sharply a point's motion is changing at t = 4 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 2t^3 - 3t^2 for t in seconds since release. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001691: A calibration log at a piston test cylinder lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a rocker arm: the two numbers add up to 7 and multiply together to give 10. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. Multiply that reading by 3, subtract 8 from the result, then add 8 back, then add 5 more. (The cylinder head is cooled by a fan drawing 15 watts, a detail that plays no role here.) That final acceleration acts on a rocker arm with a mass of 12,000 grams. What is the push this arm requires, in newtons?
w10_P4_001695: At a magnetic rail launcher test site, a technician repeats a coil-firing test 6 times. Each firing combines a baseline push worth 4 units with an extra surge worth 6 units, and adding the results from all 6 firings together gives the total acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a 159 kilogram sled. (The rail itself is mounted 2.2 meters above the floor, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this sled requires, in newtons, then multiply that number by 9. Convert what results into kilonewtons, multiply by 10, and then multiply the result by 3. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001701: The final number a hydraulic-press lab reports, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 7. That earlier figure is itself 15 less than a value that was, before that, 30 less than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules. That joule value is the energy carried by a 27 kilogram test block moving at a speed equal to the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both a 232 centimeter rod and a 28 centimeter rod with nothing left over. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001703: At a wind turbine nacelle test rig, two support cables measure 290 centimeters and 232 centimeters. Technicians want the greatest length, in centimeters, that divides evenly into both cables with nothing left over, and that length becomes the speed, in meters per second, of a 30,000 gram calibration mass. (The nacelle housing is painted with 2 liters of primer, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the energy this mass carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 8. Convert what results into kilojoules, and then multiply the result by 12. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001708: The final number a go-kart test crew logs, in kilojoules, comes from converting an energy value that is, itself, 23 less than a figure which was 2 less than an earlier energy reading, in joules, after that reading was multiplied by 3. The unmultiplied energy is what a 3,000 gram test mass carries while moving at a certain speed. That speed, in meters per second, is how fast a point on a linkage is moving at t = 1 second, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = 4t^3 for t in seconds since release. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001710: A calibration sheet at an elevator motor test rig lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a counterweight: the two numbers add up to 8 and multiply together to give 12. The correct reading is the larger of the two. That acceleration acts on a counterweight with a mass of 112 kilograms. (The elevator shaft is 18 meters tall, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this counterweight requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Multiply the result by 11, then by 2, and then by 4. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001715: At a roller-coaster launch test track, a test sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 8t, where t is the time in seconds after release. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 2 seconds and t = 4 seconds. That speed is reached by a sled with a mass of 46,000 grams. (The track's safety rail is 1.2 meters tall, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 7, then subtract 30 from the result. Convert what remains into kilojoules, and then subtract 9 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001720: The final number a robotic-arm test engineer records, in kilonewtons, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 12. That figure is itself 5 less than a kilonewton reading converted from a force in newtons, after that force was multiplied by 4. The unmultiplied force is what a 105 kilogram joint housing exerts while accelerating at a rate equal to the total acceleration gained between t = 0 and t = 3 seconds, given that the rate at which the joint's acceleration builds up -- its jerk, in meters per second cubed -- follows j(t) = 5t^2 + t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001726: At a go-kart track test bay, a kart's position along the straightaway, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds since the start. Engineers need the kart's speed at t = 1 second. That speed applies to a scale-model kart with a mass of 10,000 grams. Find the energy this kart model carries at that speed, in joules, then convert that number into kilojoules. Subtract 12 from the result, then multiply what remains by 2, and then by 6. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001727: At a piston test cylinder, a piston's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 - 4t^2, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the piston's speed at t = 1 second, and they multiply that speed by 5 to obtain the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a connecting rod with a mass of 83,000 grams. (The cylinder bore measures 9 centimeters across, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the push this rod requires, in newtons, then multiply that number by 2, then by 11, and then add 6 more. What is the final number, in newtons?
w10_P4_001739: The final number a wind-tunnel model lab logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy reading by 8. That reading, in joules before conversion, is the energy a 60,000 gram scale model carries while moving at a speed that is 13 less than a total computed earlier. That total is found by repeating a wind-gust test 8 times, where each repetition combines a baseline gust worth 6 units with an extra gust worth 2 units, and adding together the results from all 8 repetitions. (The tunnel's intake fan draws 3 kilowatts, a detail that plays no role here.) What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001741: At a hydraulic press bench, the ram's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 3t^3 + 5t^2, where t is the time in seconds after the stroke begins. Engineers need the ram's speed at t = 2 seconds. That speed applies to a ram head with a mass of 17,000 grams. Find the energy this ram head carries at that speed, in joules, then multiply that number by 2, then by 5, then by 2 again, and then by 12. What is the final number, in joules?
w10_P4_001748: At a water pump station test rig, a test slug's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 2t^2 + 2t, where t is the time in seconds after the pump starts. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds. That speed applies to a slug with a mass of 4 kilograms. (The pump housing is rated for 240 volts, a fact that plays no role here.) Find the energy this slug carries at that speed, in joules, then subtract 6 from that number. Convert what remains into kilojoules, multiply by 11, and then subtract 1 more. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001758: A calibration sheet at a centrifuge rotor bay lists two candidate acceleration readings, in meters per second squared, for a spinning arm: the two numbers add up to 7 and multiply together to give 12. Records confirm the true reading is the smaller of the two. That acceleration acts on an arm segment with a mass of 195,000 grams. Find the push this segment requires, in newtons, then convert that number into kilonewtons. Add 18 to the result, then multiply what remains by 5, and then by 6. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001759: The final number a magnetic-rail-launcher engineer logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying an earlier figure by 5, after that figure was already multiplied by 9 and increased by 5. Before those adjustments, the value was a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value, in joules, carried by a 33,000 gram sled moving at a speed numerically equal to how sharply a linkage's motion is changing at t = 2 seconds, given that its position, in meters, follows s(t) = t^3 + 2t^2 for t in seconds since release. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001760: The final number a wind-tunnel test lab reports, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 3. That figure, in kilojoules, came from converting an energy value in joules that had already been multiplied by 12 and then by 2. The unmultiplied energy is what a 38 kilogram scale model carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 4 seconds, given that the model's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = t^2 + 4t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001768: The final number a flywheel-rig technician logs, in kilojoules, is obtained by multiplying a converted energy figure by 6. That figure, in kilojoules, came from converting an energy value in joules that had first been reduced by 5 and then multiplied by 7. The unreduced energy is what a 20,000 gram flywheel segment carries while moving at a speed equal to the larger of two candidate readings on the calibration sheet -- two numbers that add up to 8 and multiply together to give 7. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
w10_P4_001769: At a satellite-thruster test bay, an engineer must select 3 nozzles out of 7 identical units on a rack for a burn test. The number of different groups of 3 she could form becomes the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a thruster housing with a mass of 115,000 grams. Find the push this housing requires, in newtons, then subtract 24 from that number, then multiply what remains by 7. Convert what results into kilonewtons, and then subtract 22 more. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001774: At a piston test cylinder, a piston's position, in meters, follows s(t) = 5t^3 - 2t^2, where t is the time in seconds after ignition. Engineers need the piston's speed at t = 1 second, and they add 29 to that speed to get the acceleration, in meters per second squared, of a connecting rod with a mass of 138 kilograms. (The cylinder is cooled by 4 liters of oil circulating through it, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the push this rod requires, in newtons, then subtract 30 from that number. Convert what remains into kilonewtons. What is the final number, in kilonewtons?
w10_P4_001779: At a model-rocket sled test track, a sled's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 2t^2 + t, where t is the time in seconds after launch. Engineers need the speed gained between t = 2 seconds and t = 4 seconds. That speed applies to a sled with a mass of 11 kilograms. (The track's guide rail is 5.5 meters long, a detail that plays no role here.) Find the energy this sled carries at that speed, in joules, then add 19 to that number, then add 9 more, then subtract 20, and then subtract 30. What is the final number, in joules?
w10_P4_001780: The final number a catapult test crew logs, in kilojoules, is 16 more than an earlier figure, which is itself 4 more than a kilojoule reading converted from an energy value in joules that had already been multiplied by 12. The unmultiplied energy is what an 8,000 gram projectile carries while moving at a speed gained between t = 0 and t = 1 second, given that the projectile's acceleration, in meters per second squared, follows a(t) = 5t^2 + 5t over that interval. What is the final number, in kilojoules?
